text.p: Following are some of the major events to have occurred on April 6 in history:
1199 - King Richard The Lionheart (Richard I) died after being wounded whilst besieging the castle of Chalus in France. He was succeeded by his brother John.
1483 - Raphael, Italian painter, born as Rafaello Sanzio. A master of Renaissance style, he decorated a large papal chamber in the Vatican - the Stanza della Segnatura. He died on this day in 1520.

1490 - Matthias I Corvinus, King of Hungary, died. King from 1458, he succeeded in binding Hungary together and occupied much Habsburg territory including Vienna. On his death all his conquests were lost.
1528 - Albrecht Duerer, German artist and engraver, died. One of the great German Renaissance artists, he was famed for his copper engravings "Knight, Death and Devil" (1513).
1580 - An earthquake badly damaged St Paul's Cathedral and other churches in London.
1652 - Jan van Riebeeck landed at Table Bay, at the Cape, South Africa, to establish a trading station for the Dutch East India Company.
1789 - George Washington was elected first president of the United States. He was the only president to be unanimously elected.
1830 - The Church of Jesus Christ of the Latter Day Saints, whose followers are known as Mormons, founded by Joseph Smith at Fayette in New York State.
1862 - In the U.S. Civil War, the Confederates under Johnston with 43,000 men surprised the Federal army under Grant at the battle of Shiloh.
1868 - In Japan, Emperor Meiji established the Charter Oath which changed the form of government and promised an assembly.
1874 - Harry Houdini, U.S. magician and escapologist, born as Ehrich Weiss. He could escape from any kind of bonds, container, prison cell or padlocked underwater box.
1890 - Anthony Herman Gerard Fokker, Dutch aircraft designer, born in Java. He founded the Fokker aircraft factory at Johannistal near Berlin in 1912.
1895 - "Waltzing Matilda", one of Australia's best-known tunes written by bush poet Banjo Paterson, was first publicly performed at a hotel in the remote northern town of Winton.
1896 - The first modern Olympic Games, revived by Baron de Coubetin, were inaugurated in Athens.
1909 - U.S. navy commander Robert Peary, leading an expedition, reached the North pole.
1917 - In World War One, the United States declared war on Germany.

1929 - Andre Previn, U.S. conductor, pianist and composer, born in Berlin. Known as a classical orchestral conductor, notably of Shostakovich, he also conducted and scored film music and arrangements especially "Gigi" and "Porgy and Bess".
1941 - In World War Two, Germany invaded Greece and Yugoslavia, and heavily bombed Belgrade.
1942 - Japan bombed India for the first time and attacked ports in Madras.
1955 - Winston Churchill stepped down as British prime minister for the last time and was succeeded by Anthony Eden.
1965 - Early Bird I, the world's first commercial communications satellite, was launched from Cape Kennedy, Florida. It became operational on June 28.
1968 - Pierre Trudeau became Liberal prime minister of Canada succeeding Lester Pearson.
1971 - Igor Stravinsky, Russian-born composer, died in New York. One of the 20th Century's leading musical figures and most famous for his ballets "The Rite of Spring" and "Petrushka".
1984 - The Cocos (Keeling) Islands in the Indian Ocean voted to integrate with Australia, ending the 150-year rule of the British Clunies-Ross family.
1992 - The European Community recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina as an independent state and war broke out between Bosnian government and local Serbs, who laid siege to the capital Sarajevo.

1994 - The Presidents of Burundi and Rwanda, Cyprien Ntaryamira and Juvenal Habyarimana, were killed when a rocket downed their plane as it landed in Rwanda. The assassinations unleashed genocide in Rwanda.
1996 - Actress Greer Garson died aged 92. Best known for her 1942 film "Mrs. Miniver," for which she won an Oscar.
